doc.title: Ran Blake interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 16, 2021

title: Legacy: The Primacy of the Ear
summary: Rowe asks about legacy; Blake names his book and the importance of ear-based teaching.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yes. Recently I had a conversation with a friend that I’ve had an almost 50-year friendship, a fellow musician, and maybe because we had some of that same brandy that you had on the plane, but we were getting sort of reminiscing about our careers and we got into the what are we leaving behind? Have we made any contributions that will outlive us? And so I guess I’m wondering, have you thought about your legacy? What do you hope will be Ran Blake’s lasting contribution?

I love a couple of — more than a couple, I love my music to be performed by others, but I think my legacy is the book. It could be longer, I could revitalize it with experiences. But as it was I had so many people like Jason Rogers helping me and so many others. I think that the ears should be used more. Now this is not my invention, in India, Africa, from grandmother to grandson, this tradition has been around us and it may have been through the beginning of Duke Ellington when starting his band in Washington. But it’s not really used well enough and I think many people are trying and there’s some wonderful music that will last and have many more implications than my own. But I do feel as an educator I’ve tried my best to get people to go back to fundamental sound and it’s more than just singing back a melody but you hear that, you get a little of the melodic rhythm, you get a sound of orchestra register, the timbre, the sound of a decay. Would that be somebody aging or would it be an inspiration of a beautiful feeling of spring that our young people have only the saddened over the years, and then they have a very early autumn.
You’re a poet also, Ran. Thank you for that.
